plan.contextChunk: This figure is a ball-and-stick model of a single sulfuric acid molecule, H2SO4, floating on a plain white field with no labels beyond the atom symbols. A yellow sphere labeled "S" sits at the center, and four red spheres labeled "O" radiate from it in a tetrahedral arrangement rendered in perspective: one up and slightly left, one out to the left, one down and toward the viewer, and one to the right. Each sulfur-oxygen bond is a cylinder colored yellow on the sulfur half and red on the oxygen half. Two of the oxygens carry a small white sphere labeled "H" on a short red-and-white bond: the upper one, whose hydrogen points up and right, and the right-hand one, whose hydrogen points up and slightly left. The other two oxygens are terminal and bare. Equal bond lengths and roughly equal angles about the sulfur make the tetrahedral geometry the thing to read off the model, while hydrogen on exactly two oxygens separates the hydroxyl pair from the pair that is not protonated. The structure is that of the compound industry manufactures in greater quantity than any other.

elements: central yellow sulfur sphere labeled 'S'
red oxygen sphere labeled 'O' at top (hydroxyl — bears H)
red oxygen sphere labeled 'O' at left (terminal, bare)
red oxygen sphere labeled 'O' at bottom, toward viewer (terminal, bare)
red oxygen sphere labeled 'O' at right (hydroxyl — bears H)
small white hydrogen sphere labeled 'H' attached to the top oxygen
small white hydrogen sphere labeled 'H' attached to the right oxygen
four sulfur–oxygen bond cylinders, each split yellow (S half) + red (O half)
two oxygen–hydrogen bond cylinders, each split red (O half) + white (H half)
text labels: 'S', four 'O', two 'H'

interactions.teaches: The four oxygens sit at tetrahedral vertices around the sulfur — only by rotating the model does the learner see that the left and bottom oxygens are the bare (terminal) pair while top and right carry the hydrogens
Clicking an oxygen classifies it: a hydroxyl oxygen flashes its O–H bond, a terminal oxygen flashes its bare S–O bond, making concrete that exactly two of the four oxygens are protonated

interactions.label: Overlay
interactions.teaches: Switching from element symbols to bond-type emphasis (S–O vs O–H) shows that the same tetrahedral framework contains two acidic hydroxyl groups among its four oxygens

demo_steps.title: Atom-label view
demo_steps.narration: The yellow sulfur sits at the center with four red oxygens at tetrahedral vertices. Two of them — the top and the right — carry a white hydrogen; the left and bottom ones are bare.

demo_steps.title: Classify each oxygen
demo_steps.narration: Click any oxygen: hydroxyl oxygens flash their O–H bond, terminal oxygens flash their bare S–O bond. Only two of the four classify as hydroxyl.

demo_steps.title: Bond-type view
demo_steps.narration: With the labels hidden and the bonds emphasized, the S–O framework and the two acidic O–H groups stand out directly — the structural basis of sulfuric acid's two ionizable protons.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Sulfur sphere radius ~0.55 units at origin; oxygen spheres radius ~0.45; hydrogen spheres radius ~0.28. S–O bond length ~1.35 units each (equal lengths); O–H bond length ~0.85 units. Oxygen directions from sulfur (normalized, approximately tetrahedral ~109.5° apart): top O ≈ (−0.35, +1, −0.35); left O ≈ (−1, +0.15, +0.4); bottom-front O ≈ (−0.4, −1, +0.75) toward the viewer; right O ≈ (+1, −0.15, −0.35). Hydroxyl pair: TOP and RIGHT oxygens; terminal pair: LEFT and BOTTOM-FRONT. The top oxygen's H points up and to the right; the right oxygen's H points up and slightly left (toward the viewer). Colors: sulfur yellow ~#d9cf22 with black 'S' label; oxygen red ~#cf1f1f with white 'O' label; hydrogen off-white ~#f5f5f5 with black 'H' label; each bond cylinder split into two half-segments colored to match its two atoms. Background plain white.
interactionPlan.notes: Use THREE.Raycaster against the four oxygen meshes for the click interaction; on select, pulse/emissive-highlight the bond (O–H if hydroxyl, S–O if terminal) and show a small hydroxyl/terminal caption. Labels should be billboied sprites (CSS2D or canvas sprites) so they face the camera while orbiting. In 'Bond types' mode hide label sprites, thicken the bond cylinders, and tint S–O bonds vs O–H bonds distinctly; restore on toggle back. Keep the white background and soft shading to match the textbook's clean ball-and-stick look.

authoredContext:
The preparation of sulfuric acid, H2SO4 (shown in the figure), begins with the oxidation of sulfur to sulfur trioxide and then converting the trioxide to sulfuric acid. Pure sulfuric acid is a colorless, oily liquid that freezes at 10.5 °C. It fumes when heated because the acid decomposes to water and sulfur trioxide. The heating process causes the loss of more sulfur trioxide than water, until reaching a concentration of 98.33% acid. Acid of this concentration boils at 338 °C without further change in concentration (a constant boiling solution) and is commercially concentrated H2SO4. The amount of sulfuric acid used in industry exceeds that of any other manufactured compound.

Sulfuric acid has a tetrahedral molecular structure.

A space filling model shows a yellow atom labeled, “S,” bonded on four sides to red atoms labeled, “O.” Two of the red atoms are bonded to white atoms labeled, “H.”

The strong affinity of concentrated sulfuric acid for water makes it a good dehydrating agent. It is possible to dry gases and immiscible liquids that do not react with the acid by passing them through the acid.
